sulfur-topical.summary: Old-school over-the-counter sulfur in masks, soaps and spot treatments that helps calm breakouts and redness for clearer skin.

quick.overview:
Topical sulfur is one of the oldest skin treatments, sold over the counter in washes, masks and spot treatments. People use it to get fewer breakouts, less redness and clearer skin, especially if they want to avoid harsher actives.

Sulfur is described as keratolytic and antimicrobial, so it helps clear pores and cut bacteria. Dermatology reviews list sulfur with sodium sulfacetamide among rosacea therapies backed by more than one randomised trial; for acne alone, the available sources include a label and a comedogenicity study but fewer controlled trials.
quick.how: It comes as a wash, mask or leave-on spot treatment, applied to breakout-prone areas or the whole face, often as a gentler alternative to stronger acne actives. Users generally treat it as part of an ongoing routine and judge results over several weeks.
quick.risks: OTC acne products carry external-use-only warnings. A randomised study found no link between sulfur and comedone formation under its conditions, and trials in scabies and hand eczema did not highlight prominent adverse effects. Sulfur products can smell strongly and may dry or irritate skin.

angle.text: Topical sulfur is an over-the-counter option in masks, soaps and spot treatments for acne, rosacea and body breakouts. Its antibacterial, keratolytic action leads to fewer breakouts and less redness, which shows as clearer skin. Rosacea trials have tested it combined with sodium sulfacetamide.

topical-finasteride.summary: Scalp-applied finasteride that blocks scalp DHT to slow hair loss and hold your hairline, with less whole-body exposure than the pill.

quick.overview:
Topical finasteride puts the hair-loss drug on the scalp as a spray, solution or gel instead of a daily pill. People use it to keep their hairline and density while limiting how much of the drug reaches the rest of the body.

Finasteride blocks type II 5-alpha-reductase, which converts testosterone to DHT, a hormone linked to follicle miniaturisation, so follicles stop shrinking and loss slows. Small randomised trials, a phase III spray trial and a systematic review report hair-count gains, and one meta-analysis found no significant efficacy difference from the oral drug. Studies also report some drop in plasma DHT.
quick.how: It is applied to the scalp on a regular schedule, often mixed with minoxidil in one product, and used long term because gains fade after stopping. Hair changes in pattern hair loss generally take months to show.
quick.risks: Oral finasteride is associated with sexual side effects, a depression warning in the US label, and discussion of persistent symptoms called post-finasteride syndrome. Topical use was designed to reduce systemic exposure but still lowers plasma DHT in studies. It is prescription-only or off-label in most settings, and concentrations and formulations vary.

angle.text: Topical finasteride is applied to the scalp to block local DHT, so follicles stop shrinking and thinning slows, helping people keep their hairline and thickness. The aim is to keep the benefit of the oral drug with less systemic exposure. Trials are smaller than for the oral version.

fluridil.summary: Topical antiandrogen sold in Europe as Eucapil that blocks androgen receptors in the scalp to slow pattern hair thinning.

quick.overview:
Fluridil is a topical antiandrogen sold in Europe as Eucapil for pattern hair loss. People look to it for slower thinning and fuller hair without lowering hormones throughout the body.

Its developers describe it as suppressing the androgen receptor locally in the scalp, so follicles are less affected by androgens, while being highly hydrophobic, easily broken down by hydrolysis and not absorbed into the body. The published evidence is a 2002 randomised trial in 43 men, which reported a higher percentage of hairs in the growth (anagen) phase than placebo and no changes in sexual function or lab values.
quick.how: It is a lotion applied to the scalp as part of a regular hair-loss routine, used by people who want a non-systemic option. Hair-cycle changes build over months.
quick.risks: The 2002 study found no irritation or sensitisation in patch tests and normal sexual function and blood values, but it was small and short, and long-term data are not available. It is not an approved drug in the US.

angle.text: Fluridil, sold in Europe as Eucapil, is a topical antiandrogen that blocks androgen receptors in the scalp, so follicles shrink less and thinning slows. People use it as a non-systemic option for fuller hair. Its clinical data come from a 2002 trial in 43 men.

caffeine-shampoo.summary: Anti-hair-loss shampoo with caffeine (Alpecin and others) that you add to a thinning-hair routine to support fuller-looking hair.

quick.overview:
Caffeine shampoos are cosmetic products sold to people with thinning hair, with Alpecin the best-known brand. They are an easy add-on to a hair-loss routine, aimed at slower thinning and fuller hair.

The idea is that caffeine absorbed at the follicles counters the effects of androgens on hair. Caffeine-based products are described as promising in lab and animal work, and one 2020 study examined a phyto-caffeine shampoo in women with female androgenetic alopecia; its results were not available in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It is used in place of a regular shampoo, left on the scalp briefly during washing, and typically combined with other hair-loss treatments. Users keep it up over months.
quick.risks: No safety information was available in the sources reviewed. These are sold as cosmetic products rather than approved hair-loss drugs, so they carry no drug-style claims.

angle.text: Caffeine shampoos such as Alpecin are marketed to people with thinning hair as an easy addition to a hair-loss routine. Caffeine at the follicles is meant to counter androgen effects, slowing thinning for fuller hair. One study has looked at a caffeine shampoo in women.

tongkat-ali.summary: Southeast Asian root extract taken as a natural testosterone booster for better training, muscle, leaner body composition and libido.

quick.overview:
Tongkat ali is a Southeast Asian root used traditionally as an aphrodisiac and now sold as a testosterone-support supplement, popular in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles. People take it hoping for better training, more muscle, a leaner look and higher libido.

The chain runs from a claimed testosterone rise to better training and body composition. A 2022 meta-analysis of small randomised trials found higher total testosterone with E. longifolia, especially in men with low levels, while a 2024 review of 27 testosterone boosters concluded most do not raise total testosterone against placebo. Erectile-function results are mixed.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily capsule or powder extract, often alongside training and sometimes stacked with other herbs such as fadogia. Users usually run it for weeks to months and judge energy, libido and gym performance.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited; a 2010 review noted gaps for commercial products, and one study found a water extract changed propranolol absorption. It is sold as a supplement, so product content varies.

angle.text: Tongkat ali is a root extract taken for higher testosterone, aiming at better training, more muscle and a leaner look. Small trials report higher total testosterone, especially in men with low levels, while broader reviews of testosterone boosters are more mixed.

fadogia-agrestis.summary: Podcast-popular African stem extract, often stacked with tongkat ali, taken for testosterone, libido and training for a more muscular, leaner look.

quick.overview:
Fadogia agrestis is an African plant whose stem extract is sold as a testosterone and libido supplement, usually alongside tongkat ali. It became widely known through podcasts and fitness social media, and people take it for better training, recovery and a more muscular, leaner look.

The chain is a claimed testosterone rise leading to better training and recovery. The research is almost entirely in rats, including a 2005 study reporting higher serum testosterone and more mating behaviour; no human clinical trial was found.
quick.how: It is taken as a capsule or powder, typically in a stack with tongkat ali, over weeks to months alongside training. Because there are no human trials, results come from user reports.
quick.risks: Rat studies have looked at testicular function and liver and kidney toxicity, and related plant species cause cardiac toxicity in livestock. Human safety data do not exist, and a 2019 analysis found supplement contents differ widely.

angle.text: Fadogia agrestis is a stem extract, often stacked with tongkat ali, taken to raise testosterone for better training, muscle and libido. The idea is a testosterone rise leading to a more muscular, leaner look. Support comes from rat studies; no human trial was found.

shilajit.summary: Himalayan mineral resin taken for testosterone, energy and recovery, with a small trial reporting higher testosterone after 90 days.

quick.overview:
Shilajit is a tar-like mountain exudate used for thousands of years in Ayurveda as a rejuvenating tonic. People take it for higher testosterone, energy and recovery, hoping for better training and a fuller physique, and sometimes for bone and collagen support.

It is made up mostly of humic substances such as fulvic acid plus minerals. A small randomised trial in healthy men aged 45 to 55 reported higher testosterone and DHEAS after 90 days of purified shilajit, and other trials have looked at bone and collagen markers. Most research uses proprietary extracts, and its exact composition and origin are not fully characterised.
quick.how: It is sold as a resin dissolved in warm liquid, or as capsules and gummies, and taken daily over weeks to months alongside training.
quick.risks: Purified products are described as generally well tolerated in small trials, while raw material may contain contaminants such as heavy metals according to general references. Content varies by source, and it is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Shilajit is a Himalayan mineral resin taken for testosterone, energy and recovery, which feed into better training and a fuller physique. One small trial in men reported higher testosterone after 90 days; physique and ageing uses rest on traditional claims and user reports.

cistanche.summary: Chinese tonic herb that bodybuilding forums list as a testosterone and DHT booster for libido, strength and recovery.

quick.overview:
Cistanche is the dried stem of a parasitic desert plant used for centuries in traditional Chinese medicine as a kidney and vitality tonic. In bodybuilding forums it is mentioned as a testosterone or DHT booster and as part of post-cycle herb stacks, taken for libido, strength and recovery.

The chain is a claimed testosterone and DHT rise leading to better strength and recovery. Research so far is mostly lab and animal work on compounds such as echinacoside and acteoside, plus a few small human trials on strength, cognition and fatigue; none found measured testosterone or DHT.
quick.how: Extracts are taken as capsules or powders, often stacked with other herbs, including after steroid cycles. Users take it daily for weeks and judge libido, energy and training.
quick.risks: Trials reported so far are small and short, and it is approved as a food ingredient in China. Long-term safety data in healthy men are limited, and wild C. deserticola is on CITES Appendix II.

angle.text: Cistanche is a Chinese tonic herb that bodybuilding forums describe as a testosterone and DHT booster, taken for libido, strength and recovery, including after cycles. Small human trials have looked at strength, cognition and fatigue rather than hormone levels.

kisspeptin.summary: Hypothalamic peptide that triggers LH release; TRT forums use kisspeptin-10 as an hCG alternative to keep the testes active.

quick.overview:
Kisspeptin is a natural signalling peptide that tells the hypothalamus to release GnRH, which drives LH and testosterone. Its fragment kisspeptin-10 is sold as a research peptide, and testosterone-therapy forums discuss it as an alternative to hCG or gonadorelin for keeping the testes active and aiding recovery after cycles, helping maintain muscle, fullness and libido.

It binds KISS1R on GnRH neurons, increasing GnRH pulses and thereby LH and FSH from the pituitary; in men, LH stimulates testicular testosterone production. Academic trials show it raises LH in volunteers, but none tests the forum use or appearance outcomes.
quick.how: Forum users describe it as a research peptide used alongside testosterone replacement or after a steroid cycle, in place of hCG, usually under clinician or self-directed protocols that vary widely.
quick.risks: It has no approved indication, and products are unregulated research chemicals. Long-term effects of repeated self-administration have not been established in the cited trials, and effects on appearance are untested.

angle.text: Kisspeptin-10 is a hypothalamic peptide that triggers LH release, and TRT users discuss it as an hCG alternative to keep the testes producing testosterone and to aid post-cycle recovery. Academic trials show it raises LH in volunteers; use alongside TRT has not been tested.

gonadorelin.summary: Synthetic GnRH that TRT users take instead of hCG to keep the testes active and limit shrinkage while on testosterone.

quick.overview:
Gonadorelin is lab-made GnRH, the brain signal that makes the pituitary release LH and FSH. On TRT forums it is used in place of hCG to keep the testes active, aiming for less testicular shrinkage and steadier hormones.

It binds GnRH receptors on the pituitary, triggering LH and FSH release. Doctors have used it for diagnostic testing and, as pulsed infusions, to restore ovulation or fertility in people with GnRH deficiency. No trial has compared it with hCG in men on testosterone, and users report mixed results.
quick.how: TRT users take it on a regular schedule alongside testosterone, as a substitute for hCG, often prescribed by clinics that offer TRT. Because it is cleared within minutes, how it is pulsed matters.
quick.risks: Documented trials are in specialist reproductive settings. In TRT use, reports are anecdotal, some users describe persistent atrophy, and continuous exposure desensitises receptors. Supply may come from clinics or compounding sources of varying regulation.

angle.text: Gonadorelin is synthetic GnRH that TRT users take in place of hCG to prompt LH and FSH release, keeping the testes active and limiting testicular shrinkage. It is established in fertility medicine and diagnostics; forum posters report mixed results in TRT.

pregnenolone.summary: The body's master steroid precursor, taken as a supplement for hormone support, mood and libido, with hopes of a leaner, more muscular look.

quick.overview:
Pregnenolone is made from cholesterol and sits at the start of the steroid pathway, leading to progesterone, cortisol, DHEA, testosterone and estrogens. It is also made in the brain. Users take it for hormone support, mood and libido, hoping that supporting hormones helps muscle and leanness.

On forums it is discussed through the 'pregnenolone steal' idea, that stress diverts it toward cortisol. Controlled trials of oral pregnenolone have been in psychiatry, such as bipolar depression and schizophrenia; none found tested testosterone, physique or appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily supplement capsule, often alongside DHEA, as part of a hormone-support routine. Users mostly judge mood, libido and energy.
quick.risks: Because it feeds several hormone pathways, effects can be unpredictable, and a forum poster advises supervision. It is sold as a US supplement with limited regulatory evaluation; long-term data in healthy users are lacking.

angle.text: Pregnenolone is the precursor to testosterone, cortisol and DHEA, and users take it to support hormone levels and, through them, muscle and leanness. Trials exist for mood and psychiatric uses; a testosterone or appearance effect from supplementing has not been tested.

yohimbine.summary: Alpha-2 blocker stimulant used in cutting stacks to release stubborn fat, aiming for a leaner face and waist.

quick.overview:
Yohimbine comes from yohimbe bark and blocks alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, raising noradrenaline activity. Cutters use it, often with caffeine and fasted cardio, to release stubborn fat and get leaner in the face and midsection. It is a common ingredient in pre-workouts and fat burners.

Proponents say alpha-2 receptors in some fat depots resist fat release and blocking them promotes lipolysis. The studies found are small topical-fat trials from 1995 on women's thighs and research uses of the drug as a stress probe; none shows oral fat loss in dieting men. Its effect is short-lived, with a reported half-life under about an hour.
quick.how: It is taken fasted before cardio, usually in a pre-workout or fat-burner or alongside caffeine, during a cut. Users combine it with a calorie deficit and judge changes in stubborn areas over weeks.
quick.risks: Documented adverse effects include anxiety, high blood pressure, fast heart rate and gastrointestinal upset, with rare severe cases. It requires a prescription in some countries and is sold as a supplement in others.

angle.text: Cutters use yohimbine, often with caffeine and fasted cardio, to release stubborn fat and get leaner in the face and midsection. It blocks alpha-2 receptors so more fat is mobilised from resistant areas. Support comes from mechanism and small studies; trials in dieting men are limited.

synephrine.summary: Bitter-orange stimulant sold as an ephedra-free fat-burner ingredient that raises fat oxidation during exercise.

quick.overview:
Synephrine is the main active amine of bitter orange extract, sold in fat burners and pre-workouts as an ephedra-free stimulant. People use it to burn more fat during workouts and get a leaner physique.

It is a sympathomimetic amine thought to act mainly on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors with weak beta effects, which differs from ephedrine. Small crossover trials in exercising adults found it increases fat oxidation during exercise after a dose; evidence for lasting fat loss is limited.
quick.how: It is taken before training, usually as part of a pre-workout or fat-burner blend, often with caffeine, during a cut.
quick.risks: Short controlled trials in healthy adults report good tolerance, while observational reports link bitter orange to blood-pressure and cardiovascular problems, mainly with stimulant stacks. It is a dietary supplement in the US.

angle.text: Bitter-orange synephrine is used in fat burners and pre-workouts as an ephedra substitute to cut body fat. As a stimulant it raises energy expenditure, and small trials show more fat oxidation during exercise, which feeds into a leaner physique. Long-term fat-loss trials are limited.

liothyronine-t3.summary: Prescription thyroid hormone that some cutters use off-label to speed fat loss; the US label carries a boxed warning against that use.

quick.overview:
Liothyronine is lab-made T3, the active thyroid hormone, prescribed for hypothyroidism and in some thyroid cancer care. Some physique communities use it off-label to speed fat loss on a cut, and one looksmax.org thread credits it with reducing eye puffiness.

T3 enters cells and binds thyroid receptors, raising the body's metabolic activity. Trials cover thyroid disease, depression and heart conditions, not fat loss or looks in healthy people. In people with normal thyroid function, supplemental hormone suppresses their own thyroid output.
quick.how: Off-label users take it as a tablet during a cutting phase, typically under a diet and training plan, sometimes with a doctor's involvement; reports are from bodybuilding forums rather than trials.
quick.risks: The US label's boxed warning says thyroid hormones should not be used for obesity or weight loss and that large doses may be life-threatening. Overdose causes hyperthyroid symptoms, heart rhythm problems and bone effects. It is prescription-only in the US.

angle.text: Some cutters use T3, a prescription thyroid hormone, off-label to raise metabolic rate, speed fat loss and reduce puffiness around the eyes and face. It is approved for hypothyroidism; the label warns against use for weight loss, and no trial tests it for appearance in healthy people.

hydroxyapatite-toothpaste.summary: Fluoride-free toothpaste built on enamel's own mineral, used to remineralise enamel and keep teeth smooth and bright.

quick.overview:
Hydroxyapatite toothpaste uses the same mineral that makes up tooth enamel, in tiny particles, as a fluoride-free way to protect and remineralise teeth. People switch to it for smoother enamel and brighter, healthier-looking teeth.

The particles are meant to deposit on enamel and fill microscopic defects in demineralised areas, supported by saliva's calcium and phosphate. An 18-month adult trial found it not inferior to fluoride at preventing new cavities, and a child trial and small sensitivity trials have also been positive. In bleaching trials it reduced sensitivity when added to peroxide; evidence that it whitens teeth by itself was not found.
quick.how: It replaces regular toothpaste in the twice-daily brushing routine, often used by people avoiding fluoride or managing sensitivity, and alongside whitening treatments.
quick.risks: Trials report no safety concerns, and the main safety debate in the field concerns fluoride rather than hydroxyapatite. Long-term, large-scale data are still limited, and fluoride remains the long-established standard for cavity prevention.

angle.text: Hydroxyapatite toothpaste deposits enamel-like mineral on teeth, remineralising and smoothing enamel so teeth look brighter and healthier. It is used as a fluoride-free option, and an 18-month adult trial found it matched fluoride for cavity prevention; whitening on its own has not been shown.

hyaluronic-acid-filler.summary: The standard reversible injectable gel that adds volume to lips, cheeks, chin, jaw and under-eyes, with visible results right away.

quick.overview:
Hyaluronic acid fillers are injectable gels used to add volume and reshape the lips, cheekbones, chin, jawline and under-eye area, and to smooth folds. The change in contour is visible right after treatment. They are the most widely used type of dermal filler, and randomized trials and meta-analyses support their effect on volume and wrinkles.

The gel physically fills space and binds water, and some studies report that it also prompts nearby skin cells to make new collagen. Results are temporary, commonly around six months or longer depending on product and area, and the gel can be dissolved with an enzyme if the result is unwanted.
quick.how: A licensed provider injects the gel in a short in-clinic session, with results seen immediately and touch-ups repeated as the filler fades. In looksmaxxing discussions it is a non-surgical option, discussed alongside surgery and fat grafting.
quick.risks: Most side effects are short-lived swelling, redness and bruising. Rare but serious complications include blocked blood vessels causing tissue death and, in the worst cases, permanent vision loss; guidelines describe emergency treatment with hyaluronidase. In the US fillers are regulated as medical devices and injected by licensed providers; provider skill matters.

angle.text: HA filler is injected to add volume and reshape the lips, cheekbones, chin, jawline and under-eye area, so the contour change is visible right after treatment. Its volume effect is well studied, and it can be dissolved with an enzyme if you want to reverse it.

glutathione-iv.summary: Injected antioxidant offered in some clinics as a skin-lightening drip, based on lab findings about melanin; reviews flag anaphylaxis and liver risks.

quick.overview:
IV glutathione is the injected form of a natural antioxidant, offered in some clinics to lighten skin and even out tone. The basis is lab work showing glutathione can interfere with melanin production.

Glutathione is proposed to inhibit tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and to shift pigment toward a lighter type. Dermatology reviews report that no rigorous trials establish that the intravenous route lightens skin and that standard dosing does not exist; oral and topical forms have small studies with variable results.
quick.how: It is given as a series of clinic drips, sometimes alongside other whitening treatments, with results judged over weeks to months. Use for cosmetic lightening is off-label.
quick.risks: Reviews associate IV use for lightening with anaphylaxis and liver toxicity concerns, and the Philippine FDA has acted on adverse-effect reports. A 2018 review did not suggest the IV route for skin lightening.

angle.text: Glutathione drips are offered in some clinics for lighter, more even skin. The idea comes from lab findings that glutathione inhibits tyrosinase and shifts melanin toward a lighter type. Reviews report limited clinical evidence for the intravenous route.

eye-massage-device.summary: Warming or vibrating under-eye massager used to ease puffiness and dark circles and brighten the eye area.

quick.overview:
Eye massage devices apply vibration, pulsing pressure or warmth around the eyes. People use them hoping for less under-eye puffiness, fewer dark circles and a brighter eye area.

The devices apply gentle mechanical stimulation and often heat to the periorbital area; the proposed benefit is better circulation and fluid drainage. The human studies that exist look at other outcomes, such as dry eye symptoms and eye blood flow; no trial found has tested under-eye appearance.
quick.how: They are used for a few minutes in the morning or evening, often with eye cream or serum, as a daily routine. Users usually check for puffiness in the mirror after use.
quick.risks: No device-specific safety problems appear in the sources; a small dry-eye trial tracked eye redness and eye pressure as safety measures. General caution applies to pressure near the eye.

angle.text: Users apply warming or vibrating eye massagers hoping to reduce under-eye puffiness and dark circles. The idea is that warmth and vibration help drain fluid and boost circulation so the eye area looks brighter. Studies have looked at dry-eye comfort; puffiness itself has not been tested.

microneedle-stamp.summary: Press-in derma stamp used to smooth scars and texture and to try for thicker brows or beard areas.

quick.overview:
A microneedle stamp is a small handheld tool with a block of short needles that is pressed into the skin. It is a form of microneedling, used in clinics and at home for scars, skin texture and sometimes eyebrow or beard areas, aiming for smoother skin and fuller growth.

The needles make tiny punctures that are proposed to trigger wound healing and collagen production and to help topical products enter the skin. Research specific to stamps is sparse: a review of ten years of Korean microneedle literature found 7 animal studies, 2 clinical trials and 10 case studies, and a stamp-delivered growth-factor treatment was reported in a 30-woman case series.
quick.how: The stamp is pressed vertically onto the area, often followed by a serum or topical, and repeated at intervals over weeks. Users apply it to scarred cheeks, brows or beard patches.
quick.risks: Any skin-puncturing device can cause irritation or infection if not kept sterile; health authorities have reported infections linked to non-clinical microneedling facials involving blood products. No controlled trials were found for brows or beards.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers press derma stamps into the skin to smooth acne scars and texture and to try for thicker eyebrows or beard areas. The needles create micro-injuries that trigger skin repair and a collagen response. Evidence comes from microneedling research in general and small case series.

microneedling-pen-electric.summary: Motorised needle pen that triggers collagen repair to smooth acne scars, texture and stretch marks, with small-trial support.

quick.overview:
An electric microneedling pen rapidly punctures the skin with fine disposable needles to trigger repair. People use it for acne scars, texture, stretch marks and sometimes hair or pigment problems, and it is a staple of looksmax skincare talk.

The needles create micro-injuries that start wound healing, release growth factors and stimulate collagen and elastin production, and the channels may help topical products penetrate. Small randomized studies report improvement in acne scars, often better when combined with peels or other agents; many trials are small and single-centre, and long-term data are limited.
quick.how: Sessions run in clinics or at home, with the pen passed over the skin followed by a topical, repeated at intervals over weeks to months. Results build gradually as skin remodels.
quick.risks: A systematic review of 51 articles and 1,029 patients described microneedling as relatively safe overall. Rare granulomatous reactions have been reported, with motorized pens and topical vitamin C implicated in most cases. Forum discussions of deep home settings are personal reports rather than clinical guidance.

angle.text: Electric microneedling pens are used for acne scars, texture and stretch marks. Rapid needle punctures start a repair and collagen response, leading to smoother scars and skin. Small trials report benefits for scars and texture.
